title: The defense attorney
hook: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev was famous for pleading his people's case before God

segments.voice: Yesterday Simcha Bunim gave us two pockets and two notes. Your line was two pockets. Which note did you reach for? Day three hundred. Three hundred days on the path.

Everyone has one friend who always takes your side. You call them furious about someone, and they're furious with you. You call them ashamed of yourself, and they say: come on, you were exhausted, anyone would have done that. Sometimes they're too generous. But you always hang up feeling like someone is on your team. More than two hundred years ago, in the town of Berditchev, in what is now Ukraine, there was a rebbe who played that role for his whole people, and he played it in the one courtroom that mattered most to him: before God.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO TAKES YOUR SIDE.` → `ALWAYS ON YOUR TEAM.` → `A REBBE BEFORE GOD.`

segments.voice: His name was Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, a student of the Maggid of Mezritch. People called him the defense attorney of Israel. The Hebrew word is sanegor, an old word borrowed from Greek, meaning an advocate. Pirkei Avot already uses the courtroom picture: every good deed you do gains you an advocate, every wrong gains you an accuser. Levi Yitzchak decided his job was always to be the advocate. There are many stories. Here's one of the best known. One morning he saw a wagon driver standing by his wagon, wrapped in his prayer shawl and tefillin, praying. And at the same time, greasing the wheels of his wagon. Anyone else might have scolded him: you're praying and greasing wheels at the same time? Levi Yitzchak looked up and said, in effect: Master of the world, look at your people. Even while they grease their wagon wheels, they're praying to you. Same scene. Two ways to see it. He always chose the second. He's remembered for arguing with God, too, out loud, on behalf of suffering people, in the tradition of Abraham pleading for Sodom and Moses pleading for Israel. That's not disrespect in Jewish tradition. It's a kind of love: taking both God and people seriously enough to argue. The stories come from Hasidic tradition and the details vary. But his reputation is solid: wherever others saw fault, he looked for the defense.
screen: `SANEGOR: THE ADVOCATE.` · `ONE ADVOCATE FOR EVERY GOOD DEED.` · `GREASING WHEELS WHILE PRAYING.` · `ARGUING WITH GOD, FOR PEOPLE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS THE DEFENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be someone's advocate. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you've been judging lately. A coworker, a relative, someone in the news, maybe yourself. Picture them doing the thing that bothers you. Now, like Levi Yitzchak, look for the defense. What's the most generous true reading? Tired? Scared? Trying, in their clumsy way? If you pray, you can speak up for them in your own words. If not, simply make their case, silently, as well as you can. The bell holds the time.
The defense attorney. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, who always pleaded his people's case before God, and found the good in what others scolded.
Your line: always the defense. Today, when you catch yourself judging someone, make their case first. Day three hundred.

howItsDone: Stories of Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev are told especially around Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days of judgment, and Jewish teaching encourages judging others favorably, l'khaf zekhut.

notes: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, 1740–1809; student of the Maggid of Mezritch. The wagon-driver story is widely told; versions differ, paraphrased.
Avot 4:11 uses praklit (advocate) and kategor (accuser); sanegor (from Greek synegoros) is the common later term. The script says Avot uses 'the courtroom picture'; confirm.
Judging favorably (dan l'khaf zekhut) is from Avot 1:6, cited in howItsDone.

Review fix: 'eighteenth-century Ukraine' was anachronistic (Berditchev was in Poland-Lithuania, then the Russian Empire; Levi Yitzchak served there from 1785 until 1809). Now 'in what is now Ukraine'.
The 'defense attorney of Israel' title and the sanegor framing are traditional epithets; confirm the Hebrew form (sanegoran shel Yisrael) if it will appear on screen.
